title: Purgatory (CCC 1030–1032)
hook: a purifying for those who die in God's friendship but not yet whole

segments.voice: Yesterday, judgment: each life seen in Christ's light, and judged on love. Your line was judged by love. What did more love look like with your person? Today, what the Church says about those who die loving God, but not yet whole. Day three hundred twenty-six.

The invitation says seven o'clock. The host is someone you love, and you've been waiting weeks for this dinner. It's ten to seven, and you've been working in the garden all day: dirt under your nails, sweat, a scratch on your arm. You're welcome as you are. The invitation is real and it isn't taken back. But at the door you might still say: give me a minute. Let me wash first. That minute, the wanting to be clean before you sit down with the one you love, is close to what the Catholic Church means by a word that often gets heard as something darker.
screen: `INVITED TO THE DINNER.` → `COVERED IN DIRT.` → `LET ME WASH FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The Catechism says that those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are assured of their eternal salvation. After death they undergo a purification, so as to have the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven. The Church calls this final purification purgatory, from the Latin purgare: to cleanse. Second, what it isn't. It isn't a second chance for someone who refused God. It isn't a smaller hell. The Catechism says it's entirely different from the punishment of the damned. Everyone in purgatory is already saved. They're on their way in. Third, where it comes from. Catholics point to Paul, who says that a person whose work burns up "shall be saved, yet so as by fire." And to the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died, and the text says: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." The Catechism says the Church has prayed for the dead from the beginning. Orthodox Christians pray for their dead too, without defining a purgatory in the same way, and many Protestants don't hold the teaching. Fourth, the fire. The Catechism, following tradition, speaks of a cleansing fire. Pope Benedict XVI took up the view that the fire might be Christ himself: that meeting his gaze burns away what's false in a person, and that the pain of it is the pain of love, and it heals. On this view, purgatory isn't about being punished enough. It's about being loved until a person is whole.
screen: `PURGARE: TO CLEANSE.` · `ALREADY SAVED, ON THE WAY IN.` · `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `THE FIRE MAY BE HIS GAZE.` · then, large: `PURIFIED BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the dead, and this time, the ones nobody names. Settle, and breathe. A few days ago you remembered someone you loved. Today, think of the others: a worn stone in an old cemetery where the name has rubbed away, a name on a war memorial you've walked past, the person who lived in your home before you. No one may be thinking of them today. If you pray, you can hold them in the old prayer for the dead, or in a few words of your own. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and wish them whole. The bell holds the time.
Purgatory. From the Latin for cleansing: the final purification, Catholics believe, of those who die in God's friendship but aren't yet whole. Today's word.
Your line: purified by love. Today, say one prayer or one good word for someone who has died, and one for someone still living who's hard to love. Day three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass, have Masses offered for loved ones who have died, and keep All Souls Day on November 2, when many visit cemeteries to pray.

fork.setup: you're Judas Maccabeus. under the coats of some of your fallen soldiers are tokens taken from idols, which the law forbade. what do you do?
options: have an offering made for them, praying for the dead.
fork.reveal: he sends an offering, and the text calls it a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead.

original.note: Latin: place or state of cleansing, from purgare, to cleanse.

trapdoor: what you thought: purgatory is a waiting room of punishment.
what it means: the final cleansing of those who die in God's friendship, already saved, on their way into heaven.
what a scholar hears: purgare; 2 Maccabees 12:46; 1 Corinthians 3:15; the councils of Florence and Trent; Benedict XVI, Spe Salvi 47.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Imagine' and drops the superlatives 'most important dinner of your life' and 'one of its most misunderstood words' and the 'most of us' claim; 'from the earliest centuries' now cites CCC 1032 ('from the beginning'); 'most Protestants' softened to 'many'; Benedict XVI's fire framed as a view he took up (Spe Salvi 47 credits it to some recent theologians); narrator no longer tells the listener 'until you're whole'; practice rewritten because day 322 already prayed for a loved one with the 'eternal rest' line, so today turns to the forgotten dead; fork setup follows 2 Maccabees 12:40 (things consecrated to idols under their coats).
